analysis.one_liner: Punjab National Bank is India's second-largest government-owned bank, taking deposits and lending to retail, agriculture, MSME and corporate borrowers across the country.
analysis.whats_happening: PNB announced Q2 FY27 results on 16 October 2026 (the day before the last price used here): standalone net profit rose 12.8% year-on-year to ₹5,532 crore, net interest income grew 10.8% to ₹11,601 crore, and the gross NPA ratio improved to 2.55% from 3.45% a year earlier. Advances grew 14.7% YoY to ₹13.41 lakh crore and management said domestic net interest margin (2.74%, up 10 bps sequentially) is already running ahead of its own 2.6-2.7% full-year guidance.
analysis.plain_terms: This is the classic government-bank turnaround story: a bank that was buried in bad loans a decade ago is now growing loans in double digits and shrinking its bad-loan pile quarter after quarter. The catch is that operating profit - what the bank earns before setting money aside for bad loans - grew only 4.2% YoY, much slower than the 12.8% rise in net profit. That gap means a meaningful chunk of this quarter's profit growth came from needing to set aside less money for bad loans, not from the underlying business suddenly getting that much better. That is a reasonable and improving trend, but it is not the same as organic profit growth, and investors should track whether operating profit catches up.
analysis.quarters: NII growth has been running near 11% YoY with margins ahead of guidance, and advances/deposits are both growing in double-to-high-single digits. Asset quality continues to improve steadily: GNPA fell from 3.45% (Sep-25) to 2.78% (Jun-26) to 2.55% (Sep-26), and NNPA is down to 0.25%. One flag from earlier in FY26: Q1 FY26 net profit had fallen sharply YoY due to a one-off higher tax outgo tied to a change in tax regime - a reminder that quarter-to-quarter profit swings at this bank have been driven as much by provisioning and tax items as by core banking income, so the operating-profit line is the more reliable one to watch.
analysis.performance_read: The uncomfortable long-term fact: PNB's stock closed at ₹116.3 on 16 October 2026, still about 47% below its November 2010 peak of ₹219.93 - meaning a holder from that peak is underwater in absolute price terms 16 years later, even before adjusting for inflation. There was a 5-for-1 stock split in December 2014; the peak and drawdown figures given here are already on a comparable (split-adjusted) basis, so the drawdown is real, not a split artifact - it reflects the decade-long NPA crisis and repeated equity dilution that PSU banks went through. That said, the recent recovery has been strong: PNB has beaten both the Nifty and its peer Bank of Baroda over the last 1 and 3 years (1Y: +3.08% vs Nifty -9.53% and peer -10.63%; 3Y: +64.39% vs Nifty +16.83% and peer +21.98%), though over 5 years it has roughly matched its peer (+180.41% vs peer's +188.34%, both far ahead of the Nifty's +25.27%).
analysis.valuation_read: At a P/E of roughly 5.9x and P/B of roughly 0.9x, PNB screens cheap against both its own history and private-sector bank peers. Why it is cheap: the market is pricing in the memory of a bank that needed repeated government-backed capital infusions and QIPs to survive its NPA cycle, plus the structural PSU discount (state ownership, slower cost discipline, periodic dilution risk). Whether that discount is still justified is a separate question - asset quality and margins have genuinely improved, but a single quarter's net-profit beat driven partly by lower provisions does not by itself prove the re-rating case; that needs operating profit, not just net profit, to keep growing.
analysis.growth_read: Growth so far is volume-led and broad-based: advances up 14.7% YoY, deposits up 9.9% YoY, global business up 11.9% YoY. Margins are also expanding (domestic NIM up 10 bps sequentially to 2.74%), so this isn't a case of growth bought at the expense of margin. The caveat is that management is now pushing into newer corporate segments - renewable energy, data centres, power transmission, M&A financing - where PNB's own underwriting track record is shorter than in its traditional retail/agri/MSME book (still ~58-59% of advances), which is worth watching given the bank's own recent history with large corporate NPAs.
analysis.health_read: Asset quality has clearly improved - GNPA 2.55%, NNPA 0.25%, both down meaningfully YoY - and capital adequacy (CRAR around 17%, not independently confirmed for this exact quarter-end) looks comfortable. For a bank, the equivalent of 'profits turning into cash' is net interest income actually collected plus a shrinking NPA book, and both of those trends are positive here. The risk that mattered most for PNB historically was business/credit risk (bad lending decisions), not balance-sheet financial risk, and while that risk has visibly receded, the push into untested corporate sectors means it hasn't disappeared - it has just quietened.
analysis.ownership_read: The Government of India is the promoter, holding 70.08% as of September 2026, a stake that has been stable through the year. The bank last diluted this via a ₹5,000 crore QIP in September 2024 at ₹103.75/share, a 3.15 percentage-point dilution done to shore up capital - a reminder that further capital raises (and dilution) remain a live possibility if growth accelerates. Pledging is not applicable to the government's holding. No well-known individual or marquee investor was found on the shareholding register from available sources - this is an institutionally and government-held stock, not one with a star-investor following.
strengths: GNPA ratio improved to 2.55% from 3.45% a year ago, and NNPA to 0.25% from 0.36%
Advances grew 14.7% YoY to ₹13.41 lakh crore, with deposits up 9.9% YoY
Domestic NIM at 2.74%, already ahead of management's own 2.6-2.7% full-year guidance
Dividend per share has risen from ₹0.64 (FY22) to ₹3.00 (TTM), tracking the profit recovery
watchpoints: Operating profit grew only 4.2% YoY versus 12.8% net profit growth - a chunk of the profit beat came from lower provisions, which cannot fall indefinitely
Stock remains about 47% below its November 2010 peak even after the recent rally - the re-rating is recent and not yet proven durable
Expansion into renewable energy, data centre and M&A financing are newer lending areas for a bank with a recent history of large corporate NPAs
Government promoter stake (70.08%) and past reliance on QIPs mean further dilution is a standing possibility if credit growth outpaces internal capital generation
analysis.one_thing: Whether operating profit growth (currently 4.2% YoY) converges with net interest income and net profit growth over the next 2-3 quarters - that would confirm the improvement is coming from the core business rather than from provisions that are running out of room to fall further.
analysis.data_notes: Q2 FY27 results (net profit, NII, GNPA/NNPA, advances/deposits growth, NIM) were cross-checked across Upstox, Business Standard, Angel One, Investing.com and Kotak Neo and are consistent. Valuation ratios (P/E ~5.9x, P/B ~0.9x, ROE ~12.9%, ROA ~1.05%) and CRAR (~17%) came from aggregator sites (Gurufocus, Moneyworks4me) rather than the company's own filing and could not be pinned to this exact quarter-end - treat as approximate and verify on Screener before quoting precisely. Shareholding figure (70.08% government stake, Sept 2026) is cross-checked across two sources. A search result referencing 'PNB Holdings' market debut in October 2026 was identified as unrelated - it refers to a Philippine entity, not this company, and was excluded.
